fields.features_heading: What the Therapist Reads Before the Evaluation
fields.features_subheading: A PT intake form built around movement: where it hurts, what brings the pain on, and what the patient wants to do again.
fields.feature_1:
Pain tied to the movement behind it

Ask the patient to pick a body region, rate the pain from 0 to 10, and name what brings it on. The therapist reads left shoulder, 5 when reaching overhead, not a blank line.
fields.feature_2:
Goals in the patient's own words

Add a question for the one activity the patient wants back, such as lifting a grandchild or running again. That answer gives the plan of care a target they chose themselves.
fields.feature_3:
Follow-up questions behind a yes

A yes to a past surgery or a current medication opens one more question asking which one and when. A patient with nothing to report skips past it and sees a shorter form.
fields.feature_4:
Every answer on the patient's record

Each submission saves to a database you own, filed under the patient's name, and the therapist opens that one record at the visit. Connect it to any clinic system with an API.
fields.feature_5:
Policies signed inside the form

Close the intake with the clinic's consent and cancellation policy, then a box where the patient signs on screen. The signature is kept with the rest of their answers.
fields.feature_6:
Source code your developer can extend

Export the full code to your GitHub repository on paid plans, then host the form on the clinic's own site. A developer can add the screens the front desk asks for next.

fields.usecase_heading: How PT Clinics Use the Intake Answers
fields.tab_content_1:
Nora's answers are in Owen's inbox before 8:30

Moraine Physical Therapy sends the intake link when a first evaluation is booked. Nora Haddad answers on her phone: right knee, pain at 6 of 10 on stairs, and a goal of climbing to her apartment without the rail. Before her 8:30 evaluation, physical therapist Owen Pryce gets an email card with those answers.
fields.tab_content_2:
One unclear field waits for Ingrid

Calder Physical Therapy asks every new patient for a photo of the front of their insurance card. The app reads the member ID, group number, and plan name into fields. On Cyrus Pell's card the plan name comes back below the clinic's confidence line. Ingrid Solberg at the front desk confirms it before his visit.
fields.tab_content_3:
Each work injury reaches billing with a claim number

A patient at Osterman Rehab who says the injury happened at work gets three more questions: employer, claim number, and adjuster email. That intake goes to billing coordinator Wynn Mercado, not the insurance queue. Of today's 4 intakes, 2 are work injuries, and both reach Wynn with their claim numbers.
fields.tab_content_4:
The surgeon's protocol arrives with the referral

Pellwood Sports PT asks post-surgery patients for the surgery date and an upload of the surgeon's referral and protocol. Elena Brooks reports an ACL reconstruction on Oct 9 and attaches both files. Post-op lead Tess Okonkwo gets an email card with the protocol before she books the first visit.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a PT Intake Form
fields.howto_description: Plan the questions the first evaluation needs, then build a PT intake form with Emergent in seven steps.
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Split the form by visit type
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Write questions the way patients talk
fields.howto_step_1_des: Write down what the treating therapist wants to know before the patient walks in, starting with the body region and the movement that brings the pain on. Each question on the form should trace back to a line on that list. Anything that traces to nothing comes out.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Open with one question about why the patient is coming in: a new injury, recovery after surgery, or an injury at work. Each answer opens only its own section. A post-surgery patient never scrolls past the work injury questions.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Ask which movements hurt and when, not for aggravating factors, and offer a short list for the body region instead of a blank box. Read each question aloud to someone outside the clinic before it goes in the form.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Map every answer to the person who acts on it. Pain and goals go to the treating therapist. The insurance card goes to the front desk, and a claim number goes to billing. Nobody has to read the whole packet to find their part.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Paste your question list and routing into a prompt. Emergent builds the form with its patient database and email alerts. Change anything by prompting again, such as moving the goal question to the first screen or adding a section for pediatric visits.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Fill it out yourself once for each visit type, using made-up patients and real-looking answers. Check that each path shows only its own section and that every alert reaches the person it names. Then open the records and confirm each answer landed where it should.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Send it with the booking confirmation
fields.howto_step_7_des: Put the link in the booking confirmation and ask for the form back a day before the visit. A patient who has not finished by then gets a reminder, and the therapist starts the evaluation with the answers already read.

faq_plan.q: What is a pt intake form?
faq_plan.a: A PT intake form is the set of questions a physical therapy clinic asks a new patient before the first evaluation. Beyond contact and insurance details, it asks where it hurts, which movements bring the pain on, and what activity the patient wants to get back to.

faq_plan.q: How do I create a pt intake form?
faq_plan.a: Describe it to Emergent's AI form builder in plain English: the sections, the questions for each type of visit, and who should get which answers. What comes back is a working form with its own patient records and email alerts. Try it as a new injury and as a post-surgery patient before the first real link goes out.

faq_plan.q: What questions should a physical therapy intake form ask?
faq_plan.a: Ask them in the order the therapist reads them. The reason for the visit comes first, with the pain behind it. Goals come next. History and insurance close the form. Keep each question to a single fact, and cut any question nobody will read before the visit.

faq_plan.q: Can one PT intake form work for every type of patient?
faq_plan.a: Yes, if the first question splits the path. Ask why the patient is booking and show only the matching section. A pediatric visit, for example, can switch the wording to a parent answering for the child. If the clinic also offers counseling, give those visits their own therapy intake form.

faq_plan.q: When should patients fill out a PT intake form?
faq_plan.a: Ask for it as soon as the evaluation is booked, and no later than the day before. Early answers give the front desk time to check insurance and any referral. A form finished in the waiting room still helps the therapist, but it leaves the desk no time to sort out coverage.

faq_plan.q: Can patients fill out a PT intake form on their phone?
faq_plan.a: Yes. The form is a web page, and the patient opens the link from the booking email on their phone. Emergent can build it as one question per screen, which keeps a long history section easier to get through on a small display.

faq_plan.q: What does a PT intake form ask that a general new-patient form does not?
faq_plan.a: It asks about movement and function. Start from a general patient intake form for contact details and medical history. Then add what a therapist works from: the body region, the activities that are hard now, how long it has been going on, and a goal for therapy.

faq_plan.q: Should a PT intake form ask for the referring doctor?
faq_plan.a: Yes, when the patient has one. Ask for the provider's name and phone number, plus an upload of the referral itself. The front desk then has it in hand before the visit. Make the question optional for patients who book on their own.

faq_plan.q: How do I update a PT intake form for returning patients?
faq_plan.a: Open the form with the last answers filled in and ask the patient to change only what is different, such as a new medication or a second injury. Emergent builds the form on a database you own, and the app can keep the earlier answers on the record next to the new ones.

faq_plan.q: Can a PT intake form serve more than one clinic location?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Put a location question near the top and send each submission to that clinic's front desk. Every response lands in one database with the location attached, and Emergent sets no response caps as patient volume grows. The same setup works for any intake form shared across sites.

plan.angle: Nine of the top 10 are clinic PDFs and packets, plus one intake software page: a sheet the patient fills on a clipboard before the first evaluation, typed into the chart later. This page names what a PT intake form should collect (the reason for the visit, pain and what brings it on, the activities that are hard now, the patient's goal) and shows the form working online in four clinic settings: a new evaluation the therapist reads before the patient arrives, an insurance card photo read into fields, a work injury routed to billing with its claim number, and a post-surgery referral that arrives with the surgeon's protocol. Everything is framed as what the clinic collects and who sees it, never as clinical, legal or compliance advice.
